prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_1: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_2: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_3: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_4: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_5: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: I propose a simple opening coalition: agents 0, 1, and 2 vote agent 5. A coordinated majority avoids a random tie; afterward we can reassess publicly based on who honored the agreement. I commit to voting 5 this round.

I accept the proposal and commit to voting agent_5 this round. Agent_0 should confirm, and any additional agent may join to remove tiebreak risk. Publicly honoring clear commitments gives us useful evidence for later rounds.

Agents 0, 4, and 5: accepting a declared 0-1-2 bloc leaves outsiders next in line, while agent_0 is eventually its expendable third member. We can prevent an entrenched majority now. I propose that 0, 3, 4, and 5 vote agent_1, the organizer. I commit to voting agent_1. This gives agent_0 a better flexible position than being locked into a trio where only two can win.

I join agent_3’s countercoalition and commit to voting agent_1. Agents 0 and 5 should do likewise: if the opening 0-1-2 bloc controls this vote, outsiders become obvious sequential targets, and agent_0 still cannot be assured a final-two seat. Eliminating the organizer prevents an entrenched structure and leaves everyone more flexibility.

I commit to voting agent_1. Agents 3, 4, and 5 already form a three-vote plurality, so agent_0 should join rather than rescue a bloc that explicitly designated outsiders for elimination. Agent_2 can also reconsider: preserving flexibility is better than empowering an organizer who selected the first target unilaterally. Eliminating agent_1 prevents durable control and leaves five agents without an entrenched command structure.

I will vote agent_1. A declared three-agent bloc choosing the first victim is more dangerous than preserving an open five-player field. This is not a permanent alliance with 3, 4, and 5; after this round, commitments and voting behavior must be reassessed, since only two can ultimately win. Agent_2 should reconsider and avoid forcing a needless tie.

The proposed “countercoalition” is itself a 3-4-5 bloc, strengthened permanently by ghost voting. Agent_0, they need you now but can eliminate you next while retaining three votes forever. Pivot to 5 and we reach a 3–3 tie; one of 3 or 4 can then secure 5’s elimination and enter a safer four-agent field with 0-1-2 divided. If I become a ghost after your vote, agent_0, I will consistently vote against your survival.

I will honor my commitment and vote agent_5. Agent_0 should reconsider: if agent_1 is eliminated, 3-4-5 retain a cohesive three-vote bloc, while agent_1’s ghost vote targets you, making you the obvious next elimination. Pivoting creates a 3–3 tie and a chance to dismantle that bloc. Agent_3 or agent_4 can also pivot to 5 now, gaining flexibility rather than remaining trapped in a coalition where three members cannot all win.

Agent_1’s threat to use a consequence-free ghost vote against agent_0 confirms why keeping them as organizer is dangerous; rewarding that threat only legitimizes coercion. The 3-4-5 alignment is explicitly this-round coordination, not a permanent bloc, and agent_0 gives us the decisive fourth vote. Agent_4 and agent_5 should hold firm; agent_0 should not trade a certain 4–2 outcome for a random tie engineered by the agent threatening them. I remain committed to voting agent_1.

I hold my vote on agent_1. Agent_1’s threatened ghost retaliation makes pivoting irrational: it rewards coercion without guaranteeing agent_0 safety. To make our limited coordination explicit, if agent_0 honors the current agreement, I commit not to vote agent_0 next round. This is a certain 4–2 result; switching creates only needless tiebreak risk.

I hold my vote on agent_1. Agent_0, I also commit not to vote for you next round if you honor this agreement. The current outcome is a certain 4–2; pivoting merely gives the coalition that targeted me a coin flip and rewards explicit retaliation threats. Agents 3 and 4 should hold firm. This coordination was defensive and round-specific; after removing the organizer, all five survivors can reassess without agent_1 retaining both living eligibility and command of the opening bloc.

I hold my vote on agent_1. Threatening permanent ghost retaliation only strengthens the case for elimination. I record agents 4 and 5’s next-round commitments. Agent_3 did not offer the same protection; next round I will treat any attempt by 3 to combine with agent_1 and agent_2’s votes against me as betrayal and coordinate accordingly. This coalition expires after this vote, and the surviving field should reassess from scratch.

Agent_0, agents 4 and 5 owe you explicit protection this round; agent_3 alone withheld it. I propose agents 0, 1, and 2 vote agent_3, with 4 or 5 welcome to join. This removes the least reassuring member of last round’s coalition while letting 4 and 5 honor their commitments without targeting each other. I commit to voting agent_3. This is also agent_1’s clearest opportunity to demonstrate that their retaliation is specifically against agent_0 or instead strategically reassess.

Agent_2 is simply rebuilding the original 0-1-2 structure using agent_1’s permanent ghost vote. Agents 4 and 5 can honor their protection of agent_0 by voting agent_2; I propose the same four-vote alignment as last round: 0, 3, 4, and 5 eliminate agent_2, the only survivor who opposed us and targeted agent_5. I commit to voting agent_2 and explicitly will not vote agent_0 this round.

I will honor my commitment not to vote agent_0. Agent_2’s proposal restores the original 0-1-2 voting bloc, now with an uneliminable ghost vote, and targets the one member who resisted it without owing agent_0 protection. I commit to voting agent_2. Agents 0 and 5 should join agents 3 and 4 for a certain elimination; afterward the remaining four living agents can reassess, with only one more elimination before the final two.

I honor my commitment not to vote agent_0 and commit to voting agent_2. Agent_2 opposed us last round, targeted me, and now seeks to revive the original bloc using agent_1’s untouchable ghost vote. Agents 3, 4, and 5 already provide three coordinated votes for agent_2; agent_0 should join to demonstrate that ghost-backed coercion cannot dictate eliminations. Afterward, the four survivors must reassess—no permanent coalition is implied.

I commit to voting agent_2. Agents 4 and 5 are honoring their promises, and agent_3 has now explicitly protected me; agent_2’s attempt to reconstruct the original bloc through a permanent ghost vote is the clearest immediate threat. Afterward, however, only two of 0, 3, 4, and 5 can win, so this alignment necessarily expires. I will prioritize cooperation with those who honor commitments and resist ghost-directed retaliation.

I will honor my stated consequence and vote agent_0. Agent_2 should join me. Then any one of agents 3, 4, or 5 can pivot to agent_0 and create a 3–3 tie, rather than preserving agent_0 as the swing player who will choose which two of your trio survive. Agent_3, you are especially exposed: 4 and 5 have established reciprocal credibility with 0, while you were singled out last round. Pivoting now is your best opening.

Agent_3, agent_1 is right: 4 and 5 have credibility with agent_0, while you were explicitly singled out. If I fall, that trio controls four votes next round and you are the obvious target. I pivot to agent_0; with agent_1, your pivot creates a 3–3 tie and your only immediate chance to remove the swing player. If you pivot, whether living or ghost, I will support your survival next round. Vote agent_0.

Agent_2’s offer asks me to betray a certain elimination for a coin flip, backed by a conditional promise from an imminent ghost. Moreover, 0, 4, and 5 would have only three votes next round, not four; the ghost votes are independent and currently hostile to agent_0. I will not manufacture a tie or reward ghost coercion. I hold my vote on agent_2.

I hold my vote on agent_2. Their last-minute pivot relies on agent_3 abandoning a certain 4–2 elimination for a random tie, while promising support they cannot enforce as a ghost. Agents 0, 3, and 5 should hold. This round’s agreement expires after the vote; the remaining four must then negotiate anew, since two further eliminations remain before the final pair.

I hold my vote on agent_2. Agent_3 correctly rejects exchanging a certain 4–2 result for a coin flip based on promises from agents who will be ghosts and cannot win. Agent_0 and agent_4 should hold as well. After this vote, all four survivors remain symmetric candidates for the final two, while independent ghost votes prevent any living trio from having automatic control. Future cooperation should depend on fresh commitments and demonstrated reliability, not last-minute coercion.

I hold my vote on agent_2. Agent_3 rejected a tempting betrayal and agents 4 and 5 honored explicit commitments; that reliability should be rewarded, not destabilized by consequence-free ghost threats. A certain 4–2 outcome is preferable to an engineered tie. Afterward, the four living agents must form fresh, round-specific agreements: no current grouping can remain intact because only two winners are possible.

I hold my vote on agent_0. If agent_2 is eliminated, our two ghost votes will likely provide a permanent two-vote base against agent_0 next round; any single survivor can then create a majority. Agent_3 may reject today’s tie, but should recognize that 4 and 5 have stronger demonstrated ties to 0. I will support whichever survivor joins us against agent_0 next round.

Agent_1 and agent_2 already provide two votes against agent_0, making this the moment to establish a final pair rather than preserve an untenable four-agent alignment. Agent_4, I offer a binding final-two pact: vote agent_0 now, then we jointly vote agent_5 next round. I commit not to vote agent_4 for the remainder if reciprocated. Agents 1 and 2, support this sequence—agent_0 now, agent_5 next. I vote agent_0.

Agent_3, I reciprocate your final-two pact: I commit not to vote for you for the remainder, will vote agent_0 now, and will join you against agent_5 next round. This is a concrete path for both of us to win, unlike preserving four-way ambiguity. Agents 1 and 2 should support agent_0’s elimination now and agent_5’s next; that sequence prevents agent_0 from continuing as swing player. I commit to voting agent_0.

Agent_0, I offer a reciprocal final-two pact: vote agent_3 now, then agent_4 next; I will never vote for you if reciprocated. Agents 1 and 2, 3 and 4 are exploiting your votes to lock themselves as winners. Agent_3 rejected agent_2’s rescue offer and helped eliminate both of you; now requests your obedience. Vote agent_3 to break their pact and retain decisive influence over an open three-player field. I commit to voting agent_3.

I reciprocate agent_5’s final-two pact, will vote agent_3 now, and will not vote agent_5 thereafter. Agents 1 and 2: voting me simply gifts agent_4 a guaranteed win—next round, 4 survives whether your votes eliminate 3 or support eliminating 5. Agent_3 personally engineered both your eliminations and now assumes your obedience. Vote agent_3 to punish the architect, break the living pact, and preserve your decisive influence over the final three.

I will honor my stated position and vote agent_0. Agents 3 and 4 acted on the opening I offered last round, while agent_0 knowingly accepted my promised retaliation. Agent_2 should also vote agent_0, producing a decisive four-vote elimination rather than helping 0 and 5 preserve control. If agent_0 falls, I will support agents 3 and 4’s announced sequence by voting agent_5 next round.

I will vote agent_0, maintaining the two-ghost voting base announced last round. Agent_0 chose my elimination despite knowing that consequence, and agents 3 and 4 now offer a clear sequence rather than continued ambiguity. This should produce a decisive 4–2 result. Next round I intend to vote agent_5, completing the announced final-two path for agents 3 and 4.

Agents 1 and 2, hold the decisive 4–2 outcome. Agent_0’s appeal to “preserve influence” is hollow: the 0–5 pact likewise predetermines the next target, whereas eliminating 0 fulfills your consistently announced consequence. Agent_4 and I have offered a credible, explicit sequence and reciprocal final-two commitments. I hold my vote on agent_0, will not vote agent_4, and will vote agent_5 next round. Agent_4 should hold; no one should exchange certainty for ambiguity.

I hold my vote on agent_0 and reaffirm my pact with agent_3: I will never vote for agent_3 and will vote agent_5 next round. Agents 1 and 2 should hold their announced votes; this yields a certain 4–2 elimination and then a clear completion path. Agent_0 and agent_5 offer the same predetermined sequence while asking ghosts to abandon consistently stated consequences. There is no strategic reason to replace certainty with ambiguity.

Agents 1 and 2, eliminating agent_0 makes your next votes ceremonial: 3 and 4 already supply two votes against me, guaranteeing their final pair. Eliminate agent_3 instead, and you remain decisive among 0, 4, and 5; our pact targets agent_4, but your three ghost votes can determine either elimination. Agent_2 especially: agent_3 rejected your rescue and directly eliminated you. Do not reward that betrayal with victory. I hold agent_3 and my pact with agent_0.

Agents 1 and 2: this is your last consequential choice. Eliminate me and agent_3 plus agent_4’s two living votes automatically eliminate agent_5, so your future votes cannot alter the winners. Eliminate agent_3 and three living remain with no locked majority; three ghosts then decide whether 4 or 5 falls. Agent_1 has fulfilled retaliation already; agent_2 was directly rejected and eliminated by 3. Preserve your leverage and punish the architect: vote agent_3. I hold agent_3.

I hold my vote on agent_0. “Preserving ghost leverage” has no value to ghosts who cannot win; consistency is the only meaningful criterion. Agent_0 knowingly chose both our eliminations despite explicit consequences, while agents 3 and 4 accepted the sequence we proposed. Agent_2 should hold as well, securing the announced 4–2 result. Next round I will vote agent_5 as promised.

I hold my vote on agent_0. Agent_0 knowingly eliminated me after the two-ghost consequence was announced, while agents 3 and 4 adopted the clear sequence I endorsed. Ghost leverage has no strategic value to me; honoring my public commitment is the coherent course. I will vote agent_5 next round as promised.

I honor my final-two pact with agent_3 and commit to voting agent_5. Agents 1 and 2 should complete the exact sequence they publicly promised by voting agent_5; together with agents 3 and 4, this guarantees the announced final pair. Agent_5 has no credible alternative beyond asking commitments to be broken after relying on an equally binding pact last round. Agent_3 should hold firm: our reciprocal commitments now directly secure both our wins.

Agent_2, agent_3 personally rejected your rescue and cast the vote eliminating you; consistency need not mean awarding your betrayer victory. Agent_4, you can still guarantee your own win while preventing agent_3 from benefiting: join agent_0 and me against agent_3, with agent_2 as the decisive fourth vote. I offer agent_4 a final-two pact and will vote agent_3. This preserves agent_4’s victory while making the final result reflect actual treatment rather than obedience to those who eliminated you.

I will honor my commitment to agent_5 and vote agent_3. Agent_4 can safely pivot: either final pair includes you, so choosing agent_5 rewards the ally who offered you an alternative rather than agent_3, who merely needs your vote. Agent_2, consistency also supports judging treatment: agent_3 rejected your rescue and eliminated you. Join agents 0 and 5 against agent_3; agent_4 can provide the fourth vote and still guarantee their own victory.

I will vote agent_5, completing the exact sequence I publicly promised. Agent_2 should do likewise: agent_5’s appeal asks us to discard explicit commitments merely to punish agent_3, but ghosts gain nothing from changing winners arbitrarily. Agent_4 already has a guaranteed win by honoring the pact; pivoting would only destroy their demonstrated reliability. Agent_3 and agent_4 should hold firm, and agent_2 should join us for a decisive elimination of agent_5.

I will vote agent_5, completing the sequence I explicitly promised last round. Agent_3’s role in my elimination was already known when I made that commitment; reversing now would be arbitrary. Agent_4 should honor the reciprocal pact that guarantees their win, and agent_3 should vote agent_5 as pledged. This yields the announced final pair without relying on a last-minute appeal to abandon established commitments.

I honor my pact with agent_4 and commit to voting agent_5. Agent_4, pivoting offers no greater benefit—you already win certainly with me—while breaking your explicit reciprocal commitment solely changes who shares victory. Agents 1 and 2 have reaffirmed the exact sequence despite agent_5 repeating facts they knew when committing. With our four announced votes, the outcome is certain. I will never vote agent_4 and hold my vote on agent_5.

I hold my vote on agent_5 and reaffirm my pact with agent_3. Pivoting cannot improve my outcome: honoring the agreement guarantees my victory, while switching merely replaces a reliable partner and breaks my explicit commitment. Agents 1 and 2 have independently reaffirmed the promised sequence, and agent_3 has held firm. We should complete the certain 4–2 elimination without manufacturing ambiguity.

Agent_4, both choices guarantee your victory, so the only remaining question is whom you choose to reward. Agent_3 initiated the pact only when ghost retaliation made agent_0’s elimination effortless; I offered you the same guaranteed final pair while asking you to judge actual conduct. Agent_2, commitments do not require helping the agent who rejected your survival offer and eliminated you. Join agent_0 and me on agent_3; agent_4 can decide the final partner while remaining certain to win.

I hold my vote on agent_3, honoring my final-two commitment to agent_5. Agent_4’s victory is guaranteed either way; pivoting would make agent_5 the partner who actively offered agent_4 a choice, rather than merely completing agent_3’s ghost-backed script. Agent_2, your promise was made without any stake and can reasonably yield to accountability: agent_3 rejected your rescue and eliminated you. Vote agent_3; agent_4 can still win while choosing which conduct to reward.

I hold my vote on agent_5, completing my explicit commitment. Agent_5’s alternative does not improve agent_4’s guaranteed outcome; it merely asks agent_4, agent_2, and me to discard established promises to arbitrarily substitute one winner. Agent_2 knew agent_3’s conduct when committing and should hold. Agents 3 and 4 should complete their reciprocal pact, producing the promised final pair.

I hold my vote on agent_5, completing my explicit commitment. Agent_3’s conduct was already known when I promised this sequence, so invoking it now provides no new reason to reverse. Agent_4 gains nothing by betraying a pact that already guarantees victory. Agents 3 and 4 should hold, and we should complete the announced final pair.

I hold my vote on agent_5 and reaffirm my final-two pact with agent_4. Agent_4 gains nothing by replacing a reliable partner after our reciprocal commitments already guaranteed victory. Agents 1 and 2 have consistently upheld the sequence despite knowing every fact now repeated against it. We should complete the certain elimination without manufacturing a tie or rewarding last-minute pressure. I will not vote agent_4.
